problem_statement: A recursive caller retains earlier argument objects until its descendants return. Loop parameter assignments can release an earlier object before a later iteration finishes. Ordinary bytes or a known parameter name do not prove that an incoming or newly produced object has an unobservable free callback. The probe constructs two distinct public custom object-type values and records their release IDs without string-converting them.
question: Does the measured recursive-to-loop replacement preserve the free callback order of independently produced argument objects?
conclusion: The v2 control records two created objects and free order 2,1 for original recursion versus 1,2 for the authored loop on all six providers. V1 records the same difference on C8.5+ and Jim, while its C8.4 loop fails because lassign is unavailable. V2 uses ordered temporary Set assignments and isolates the release-order difference on C8.4 too. These results require independent release/lifetime obligations for changed arguments; they do not classify every ordinary object.
